subject: glessner_frances_m_1904

shot.build: stage, tree f9d353b45 + 8 uncommitted figure file(s)

silhouette.what: Silhouette and fit of the clothes
silhouette.note: Since the tailoring fix (human-gown.js, T-3553 round 3) the skirt is close over the hips and flares from about the knee to a hem about 1.5 times the hips' half-width (64 cm across, was 83), a little fuller behind: at 3 m it reads as the Met's gored skirt and the Easter skirts, no longer a crinoline. Since round 4 the skirt driver hangs this cut as a close walking skirt (human-skirt.js CLOSE): on the walk the hem's fore-aft span grows 26 cm on the mean over the step (was 33) and 36 at the most (was 42); it no longer stays swung out between steps, but at heel strike and toe-off it still reaches about 21 cm past standing over the leading toe and the trailing heel, which is how far the gait layer's step carries the feet. Jacket to the hip with a short peplum reads as the Met coat cut shorter.

folds.note: Seven gore seams are drawn as seams pressed open (T-3553 round 4): each a valley 1 cm deep on the column of the cloth's own points nearest the seam's line, with a low ridge (5 mm) one point to either side, so the light draws a dark and a light line down each seam; at 3 m they now show as fine vertical lines on the lit side of the skirt and down the back, as the Met skirt's seams do in its photograph, though still faint in black wool on the shadowed side and fainter than the Met's studio light makes them. Below the knee the flare falls into soft folds (fourteen at the near level, seven at the next), with two rows of black braid at the hem; the folds show as a fluted hem edge. They are fixed folds that ride with the skirt, not folds that break as the walk changes; the far levels (past 20 m) carry the cut but no seams or folds.

hat_hair.note: A broad dark hat trimmed high with grey plumes over drawn-up hair: the Easter crowd and Mrs. Fairbanks wear the same kind, hers paler and heaped higher.

skin.note: Monochrome prints. Face and hands read at 3 m; the hands are warmer (orange) in the stage light than the face.

hands.note: Clasped in front at the waist; the crossed fingers are bulky at 3 m. The pictures show gloved or bare hands at the sides or raised.

stance.what: How the figure stands or sits
stance.note: Upright, feet hidden under the skirt, as the matrons stand.

motion.note: Mid-stride the skirt swings as one piece and the legs never show (test_human_skirt and test_human_gown hold it on the cut skirt, clear by 2 cm or more). Since round 4 the hem breaks forward over the leading foot and drops back with it rather than swinging fore and aft as a bell (mean span past standing 26 cm, was 33); at the moment the toe lifts it still stands further forward than the Easter women's appear to, because the step itself is long. The strip is shot on the stage, following her.

differences.picture: Gored skirt close at waist and hips, flaring from about the knee (Met 1902 suit); Easter 1904 skirts nearly columnar to the ground.
differences.ours: Close over the hips, flaring from about the knee to a hem about 1.5 times the hips' half-width (64 cm across, was 83), a little fuller behind; on the walk the hem breaks forward over the leading foot and drops back with it (a close skirt, not a bell: 26 cm mean span past standing, was 33), still reaching about 21 cm forward at heel strike.

differences.picture: Gore seams and braid at the hem (Met); folds at the hem when walking (Easter).
differences.ours: Seven gore seams drawn as seams pressed open (a 1 cm valley between two low ridges), which read as fine vertical lines at 3 m on the lit side and down the back, still faint in shadow; soft fixed folds below the knee (near levels) and two rows of black braid at the hem; the folds do not change with the stride.

differences.picture: Tall cream lace standing collar and a lace jabot falling from it (Fairbanks; Met bodice yoke).
differences.ours: Cream lace (net and flowers drawn on the cloth) over the standing collar, the pleated jabot and the top of the front; the cloth below brought up to cream. The collar is the asset's height, a little lower than Mrs. Fairbanks's, and the jabot is pleated cloth with the lace drawn on it, not a falling frill.

differences.picture: Lace frills at the wrists (Fairbanks); braided cuffs on the Met coat.
differences.ours: A cream lace frill flaring from inside each sleeve's end over the wrist (near levels, within 20 m), and soutache braid round the coat's cuffs.

differences.picture: Met coat to the upper thigh, lapels, buttoned below the bust, braid at cuffs and hem; Fairbanks coat open over a pale front.
differences.ours: Black jacket to the hip with a peplum, closed, no braid; pale front shows only as a narrow V.

differences.picture: Black wool suit (Met, in colour); dark coats in the monochrome prints.
Broad hat heaped with pale plumes (Fairbanks), broad hats trimmed high (Easter).
differences.ours: Broad black hat, grey plumes; less heaped, darker plumes.

_how: verdict is unreviewed | differs | matches, set by whoever laid the stills beside the pictures; each checklist item is {what, status, note} with status open | reads | not shown | within tolerance | owner ruling — open when a visitor would see the figure is not the pictures’ kind of person in that respect. The first figure of each role is the owner’s call (the plan’s "Your call"); later figures of the role are held to the one he approved. A reshoot of a changed figure (bound) sets the verdict back to unreviewed.
